or_k_the_dihedrals.blurb: The Dihedrals is one of the most visited sections of Smith Rock, set on the front side of the park between Asterisk Pass and the Four Horsemen and easy to pick out from the main lot. The steep faces and corners are volcanic tuff, and the climbing leans toward bolted lines with a smaller number of crack and corner routes that take gear. Difficulty spreads from easy slabs up to some of the hardest lines in the park, though a large share of the routes sit in the low 5.12 range, so it suits strong sport climbers best. Expect company on the popular routes, particularly on weekends. Summers are hot and winters cold, so spring and fall tend to be the comfortable seasons.
or_k_the_dihedrals.approach: From the main lot, cross the footbridge and follow the River Trail to the left for about a quarter mile, then turn uphill toward the base once you are past Morning Glory Wall.

or_garden_cliffs.blurb: Garden Cliffs is a small forested sport crag in the Willamette Valley foothills near Sweet Home, a short walk from a roadside boulder area. The walls run roughly 30 to 70 feet and split into three sections divided by gullies: the main cliff, a shorter wall, and a newer corner still being developed. Almost everything is bolted, often with a high first bolt that calls for a stick clip, and most routes fall between 5.10 and 5.12 with a few harder and a handful of easier ones. The main cliff stays shady much of the day and some lines dry quickly after winter rain, while others seep into summer. Holds can be brittle in places, and the trail gets brambly, so bring clippers.
or_garden_cliffs.parking_note: Along Quartzville Drive east of Sweet Home, use the small pullout directly opposite the trailhead. It only fits a few cars, so squeeze in tightly and leave room for others.
or_garden_cliffs.approach: The trail leaves the road about 80 yards from the pullout and climbs a short way to the base. Blackberries can crowd the path.

or_downstream_boulders.blurb: These are the basalt boulders spread along the Deschutes River below Cline Falls, a few minutes from Redmond. The problems are scattered among clusters with names like the Golf Boulder, Pumpkin Boulder and River Spot, and range from easy warm-ups through a busy V2 to V4 middle ground, with a few much harder lines. Mind the landings and the river's edge, and stay out of the water near the falls just downstream, which are dangerous. The area gets shade for much of a summer day, making it a handy escape on warm afternoons. The river runs higher in fall and winter, which can change which way down to the boulders is easiest.
or_downstream_boulders.parking_note: Use the big gravel pullout on the north side of Highway 126, directly across from the entrance to the state viewpoint, about four miles west of Redmond.
or_downstream_boulders.approach: Take the trail down to the river and walk downstream. An easy gully about 100 yards below the falls drops to the boulders; farther on there are other ways down.

or_zz_upper_gorge.blurb: The Upper Gorge is a quiet stretch of basalt columns on the Crooked River at Smith Rock, upstream of the Lower Gorge. The columns are mostly sealed, so there is little crack climbing and nearly all the routes are bolted, with a few traditional lines. The climbing is technical and subtle, rewarding footwork, balance and body position over brute strength, and the bulk of it falls between 5.10 and 5.13. The wall heats up in the sun and friction matters, so cooler days work best. The strip along the river is narrow and overgrown with reeds, nettles and poison ivy, and the land is partly private, so keep voices down and take care of the vegetation.
or_zz_upper_gorge.approach: There are several ways in along the narrow, overgrown corridor beside the river, and none is formal. Expect brush, nettles and poison ivy, and wear long pants.

pa_powercut_the.blurb: The Powercut is a ridge-top cluster of sandstone boulders in Hunter's Rocks, at the southwest tip of Rothrock State Forest in central Pennsylvania. It is named for the open swath cut through the trees for power lines, which makes the boulders easy to spot. The rock has good friction and plenty of pockets, and the problems cover a very wide range, from friendly V0 to V2 climbs that make up most of the count up to a few serious lines in the double digits. It is a good place for a mixed group. Parts of the ridge sit on private land where climbing is not welcome, so stay with the public boulders and park considerately.

pa_g2_2.blurb: G2 is a small boulder field on state game lands just outside Black Lick, on the south side of Black Lick Creek in southwestern Pennsylvania. Roughly fifty problems are spread over about fifteen boulders, many of them moderate lines with comfortable heights and gentle top-outs, plus a few tall, serious ones for experienced climbers. The warm-up boulders near the entrance are a good place to start. Grades here are still being sorted out, so treat the numbers loosely. It is a real walk in, just over a mile, with two open clearcuts along the way, and the land is shared with hunters, so wear bright orange during hunting seasons.
pa_g2_2.parking_note: A small game lands lot sits where Schoolhouse Road, Fisher Lane and Ruggieri Road meet and holds about four or five cars. If it is full, continue up Ruggieri Road, keeping the gate and the lane clear.
pa_g2_2.approach: Follow Ruggieri Road, go through the first gate on the left, keep right at the stone wall, and cross two clearcuts to a gas well. A footpath past it leads down into the boulders.

qc_elizabeth_boulder.blurb: Elizabeth is one of the named boulders in Les Dames, the main bouldering zone in Val-David in the Laurentians, and sits close to where you enter the trail network of the regional park. The Laurentian granite gives technical, balance-oriented problems, and the boulders here offer everything from a gentle slab at the easy end to a handful of harder lines, so it is a good first stop for a mixed group. The walk is only a few minutes and crowds are generally light.

tn_back_nine.blurb: The Back Nine is one zone of Stone Fort, the compact sandstone boulder field on Mowbray Mountain near Chattanooga, tucked in woods beside a golf course. Iron rails run through many of the boulders, and the problems mix slopers, crimps and technical faces across a full range of difficulty, from easy lines through the mid grades to a number of very hard problems. The boulders sit on private land beside the golf course, so follow the owner's arrangements for parking and access. Cool, dry days are best for friction on sandstone.
